questions.question: The necessary condition to diagonalize a matrix is that
options: all its eigen values should be distinct
its eigen vectors should be independent
its eigen values should be real
questions.explanation: A square matrix A of order n is diagnalizable if and only if it has n linearly independent eigen vectors. \[\boxed{\text{(B) its eigen vectors should be independent}}\]

questions.question: \(\lim_{x \to \dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{\sin 2\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}{x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}} = \underline{\hspace{1cm}}\)
questions.explanation:
We need to evaluate the following limit: \[L = \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sin 2\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{x - \frac{\pi}{4}}\]
Method 1
Let us use the substitution method to simplify the limit. Let \(t = x - \frac{\pi}{4}\). As \(x \to \frac{\pi}{4}\), it implies that \(t \to 0\). Substituting these values into the limit expression: \[L = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin(2t)}{t}\] To use the standard limit identity \(\lim_{\theta \to 0} \frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1\), we multiply and divide the denominator by \(2\): \[L = \lim_{t \to 0} \left[ 2 \cdot \frac{\sin(2t)}{2t} \right]\] \[L = 2 \cdot \lim_{t \to 0} \left[ \frac{\sin(2t)}{2t} \right]\] \[L = 2 \cdot 1 = 2\]
Method 2
As \(x \to \frac{\pi}{4}\), the given limit is in the indeterminate form of \(\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\). Therefore, we can apply **L'Hospital's Rule** by differentiating the numerator and denominator with respect to \(x\): \[L = \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\frac{d}{dx}\left[\sin 2\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]}{\frac{d}{dx}\left[x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right]}\] \[L = \lim_{x \to \frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{2 \cos 2\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{1}\] Now, substituting \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\): \[L = 2 \cos 2\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\] \[L = 2 \cos(0) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2\]
Thus, the correct option is D. \[\boxed{\text{(d) }\ \ 2}\]

questions.explanation: Applying KCL at node \(A\), \[\frac{V_A}{2}+\frac{V_A-V_B}{10}=5\] \[5V_A+V_A-V_B=50\] \[6V_A-V_B=50 \tag{i}\] Applying KCL at node \(B\), \[\frac{V_B}{5}+\frac{V_B-V_A}{10}=2\] \[2V_B+V_B-V_A=20\] \[-V_A+3V_B=20 \tag{ii}\] Solving (i) and (ii), \[V_A=10\,\text{V},\qquad V_B=10\,\text{V}\] Hence, the current through the \(5\,\Omega\) resistor is \[I=\frac{V_B}{5} =\frac{10}{5} =2\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) 2 A}}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: Two identical 2-port networks with \(y\)-parameters \(y_{11} = -y_{12} = -y_{21} = y_{22} = 1\text{S}\) are connected in cascade. The overall \(y\)-parameters will satisfy the condition
questions.explanation: Convert the \(y\)-parameters to \(ABCD\) parameters, multiply the matrices, and convert back to \(y\)-parameters. Given \(y\)-parameters for each identical network: \[[y] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\,\text{S}\] The conversion from \(y\)-parameters to \(ABCD\) parameters is: \[A = -\dfrac{y_{22}}{y_{21}}, \quad B = -\dfrac{1}{y_{21}}, \quad C = -\dfrac{\Delta y}{y_{21}}, \quad D = -\dfrac{y_{11}}{y_{21}}\] Where \(\Delta y = y_{11}y_{22} - y_{12}y_{21} = (1)(1) - (-1)(-1) = 0\). \[A = -\dfrac{1}{-1} = 1, \quad B = -\dfrac{1}{-1} = 1, \quad C = -\dfrac{0}{-1} = 0, \quad D = -\dfrac{1}{-1} = 1\] So, \[[ABCD] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]. For two identical networks in cascade, multiply the matrices: \[[ABCD]_{total} = [ABCD] \times [ABCD] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] Convert back to \(y\)-parameters using: \[y_{11} = \dfrac{D}{B}, \quad y_{12} = -\dfrac{\Delta ABCD}{B}, \quad y_{21} = -\dfrac{1}{B}, \quad y_{22} = \dfrac{A}{B}\] Where \(\Delta ABCD = AD - BC = (1)(1) - (2)(0) = 1\). \[y_{11} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5\,\text{S}, \quad y_{12} = -\dfrac{1}{2} = -0.5\,\text{S}, \quad y_{21} = -\dfrac{1}{2} = -0.5\,\text{S}, \quad y_{22} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5\,\text{S}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) $y_{12} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\,\text{S}$}}\]

questions.question: The discrete LTI system with the following impulse response is non-causal.
questions.explanation:
Condition for causality of a LTI system:
\[h(n) = 0; \quad n < 0\] (i) From option (A): \(h(n) = a^n u(n-2)\) This signal will exist only for \(n \geq 2\) i.e., for \(n < 0\), \(h(n) = 0\). Therefore, it is causal. (ii) From option (B): \(h(n) = a^{n-2} u(n)\) This signal will exist only for \(n \geq 0\) i.e., for \(n < 0\), \(h(n) = 0\). Therefore, it is causal. (iii) From option (C): \(h(n) = a^{n+2} u(n)\) This signal will exist only for \(n \geq 0\) i.e., for \(n < 0\), \(h(n) = 0\). Therefore, it is causal. (iv) From option (D): \(h(n) = a^n u(n+2)\) This signal exists only for \(n \geq -2\) i.e., for \(n < 0\), \(h(n) \neq 0\). Therefore, it is non-causal. Hence, the correct option is (D). (D) \(a^n u(n+2)\)

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The impulse response of a discrete LTI system is \(a^n u[n]\). Its step response is given by
questions.explanation:
Given \(x(n)=\delta(n)\ \xrightarrow{h(n)}\ y(n)\). By the convolution property, \(y(n)=x(n)\otimes h(n)\ \xrightarrow{\text{Z.T.}}\ Y(z)=X(z)H(z)\). With \(x(n)=\delta(n)\leftrightarrow 1\) and \(h(n)=a^{n}u(n)\leftrightarrow \dfrac{z}{z-a}\), \[H(z)=\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)}=\frac{z}{z-a}.\] For a unit-step input \(x_1(n)=u(n)\leftrightarrow \dfrac{z}{z-1}\), \(\text{ROC}:|z|>1\). \[Y_1(z)=\frac{z}{z-1}\cdot\frac{z}{z-a}
=\frac{1}{1-a}\cdot\frac{z}{z-1}+\frac{a}{a-1}\cdot\frac{z}{z-a}.\] Taking the inverse Z-transform, \[y(n)=\frac{1}{1-a}u(n)+\frac{a}{a-1}a^{n}u(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}a^{j}.\] A) \(\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{n} a^{j}\)

questions.question: A sample and hold circuit have two buffers one at input and other at the output. The primary requirements for the buffers are
options: The input buffer should have high slew rate and output buffer should have low bias current.
The input buffer should have low bias current and output buffer should have high slew rate.
both the buffers should have low bias currents.
both the buffers should have high slew rate.
questions.explanation: In a sample-and-hold circuit, the input buffer drives the hold capacitor during the sampling interval, while the output buffer isolates the capacitor from the load during the hold interval. The input buffer should charge the hold capacitor quickly. Hence, it must have a high slew rate. The output buffer should draw negligible current from the hold capacitor to minimize voltage droop during the hold period. Hence, it must have a low input bias current. \[\boxed{\text{(a) The input buffer should have high slew rate and the output buffer should have low bias current}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: Microprocessor 8085 regains control of the bus
options: after half-clock cycle after HLDA goes low
after half-clock cycle after HLDA goes high
questions.explanation:
For DMA operation:
  1. Once the HOLD signal is received, the microprocessor completes the current machine cycle and generates the HLDA signal. After one clock cycle, it releases the address and data buses to the external device.
  2. Once the DMA operation is completed, the HOLD signal becomes low, and the microprocessor then makes the HLDA signal low. After this, one half clock cycle later, the microprocessor takes back (regains) the address and data buses from the external device.
\[\boxed{(C)\text{ after half-clock cycle after HLDA goes low}}\]
Key points
  • HOLD is an input signal requesting the microprocessor to relinquish the buses for DMA operation.
  • HLDA (Hold Acknowledge) is the output signal confirming that the buses have been released.
  • The microprocessor releases the buses one clock cycle after asserting HLDA, and regains them one half clock cycle after HLDA goes low.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: In 8085 microprocessor, CY flag may be set by the instruction
questions.explanation:
This question concerns the effect of various 8085 instructions on the processor flags. INX and DCX: During the execution of INX and DCX, none of the flags are modified. CMA: During the execution of CMA (Complement Accumulator), none of the flags are modified. ANA: The contents of the accumulator are logically ANDed with the contents of a register or memory. During the execution of ANA, the Carry flag is reset and the Auxiliary Carry (AC) flag is set. SUB: The contents of the operand (register or memory) are subtracted from the contents of the accumulator, and the result is stored in the accumulator. All flags are modified to reflect the result of the subtraction; the Carry flag is the complement of the actual borrow/carry generated. \[\boxed{(A) \text{ SUB}}\]
Key points
  • INX, DCX, CMA do not affect any flags.
  • ANA resets the Carry flag and sets the AC flag, while modifying S, Z, P flags based on the result.
  • SUB affects all flags (S, Z, AC, P, CY), with the Carry flag representing the complement of the borrow.

Consider the open-loop transfer function \[G(s)=\frac{s+1}{s(s-1)}\] The Nyquist contour \(C\) is shown in the figure. The contour has an indentation to the left of the pole at the origin.

Draw the Nyquist plot for the given system by mapping the contour \(C\).
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
The open-loop transfer function is \[G(s)=\frac{s+1}{s(s-1)}\] The poles of the open-loop transfer function are \(s=0, 1\) The given Nyquist contour contains an indentation around the pole at the origin towards the left.
SegmentMapping
Segment--I\(j0^+\rightarrow j\infty^+\)
Segment--II\(j\infty^+\rightarrow j\infty^-\)
Segment--III\(j\infty^-\rightarrow j0^-\)
Segment--IV\(j0^-\rightarrow j0^+\)
img/ch7_nyquist_plot/7_01_1_1.png Segment--I: Put \(s=j\omega\) \[G(j\omega) = \frac{1+j\omega} {j\omega(j\omega-1)}=\frac{\sqrt{1+\omega^2}} {\omega\sqrt{1+\omega^2}}~\angle\tan^{-1}\omega -90^\circ -\left(180^\circ-\tan^{-1}\omega\right)=\frac{1}{\omega}~\angle-270^\circ+2\tan^{1}(\omega)\] \[G(j0^+) = \infty~\angle-270^\circ \qquad \text{and} \qquad G(j\infty^+) = 0~\angle-90^\circ\] On rationalizing the given transfer function, we get, \[G(j\omega)=-\frac{2}{1+\omega^2}+j\,\frac{(1-\omega^2)}{\omega(1+\omega^2)}\] \[\Re\{G(j\omega)\}=-\dfrac{2}{1+\omega^2} \qquad \Im\{G(j\omega)\}=\frac{1-\omega^2}{\omega(1+\omega^2)}\] Here, \(\Re\{G(j\omega)\}<0\) for every \(\omega>0\) But, \(\Im\{G(j\omega)\}>0\) for \(\omega<1\) and \(\Im\{G(j\omega)\}<0\) for \(\omega>1\) The nyquist plot cuts the real axis when \(\omega=1\) and at: \[G(j1)H(j1)=-\frac{2}{2}=-1\] Therefore, the nyquist plot crosses the real axis at \((-1, j0)\)
\(\omega\)\(\Re\{G(j\omega)\}\)\(\Im\{G(j\omega)\}\)Quadrant
\(\omega<1\)\(-\)\(+\)Quadrant - \(II\)
\(\omega>1\)\(-\)\(-\)Quadrant - \(III\)
Segment--II: Put \(s=Re^{j\theta}\) where, \(R\rightarrow\infty\) and \(\theta:\) \(+90^\circ\) to \(-90^\circ\) in Clockwise Direction \[G(Re^{j\theta})=\frac{Re^{j\theta}+1}{Re^{j\theta}(Re^{j\theta}-1)}\] As \(R\rightarrow\infty,\) then, \(Re^{j\theta}+1\approx Re^{j\theta}\) and \(Re^{j\theta}-1\approx Re^{j\theta}\) \[G(Re^{j\theta})H(Re^{j\theta})\approx \frac{Re^{j\theta}}{R^2e^{j2\theta}} = \frac1R\,e^{-j\theta}\] As \(R \rightarrow \infty\), then, \(\dfrac{1}{R} \rightarrow0\) As \(\theta:90^\circ\rightarrow-90^\circ,\) then \(-\theta:-90^\circ\rightarrow90^\circ\) Therefore, Segment-II maps to a semicircle of approximately zero radius about the origin and is traced in the anticlockwise direction from \(-90^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\) Segment--III: Segment--III is the mirror image of Segment--I. Segment--IV: Put \(s=re^{j\theta}\) where, \(r\rightarrow0\) and \(\theta:-90^\circ\rightarrow90^\circ\) in Clockwise direction \[G(re^{j\theta})=\frac{re^{j\theta}+1}{re^{j\theta}(re^{j\theta}-1)}\] As \(r\rightarrow0\), then, \(re^{j\theta}+1\approx1\) and \(re^{j\theta}-1\approx -1\) \[G(re^{j\theta})H(re^{j\theta}) \approx -\frac1{re^{j\theta}} = \frac1r\,e^{j(\pi-\theta)}\] As \(r \rightarrow 0\), then, \(\dfrac{1}{r} \rightarrow \infty\) As \(\theta:-90^\circ\rightarrow90^\circ,\) then \(\pi-\theta:270^\circ\rightarrow90^\circ\) Therefore, Segment-IV maps to an infinite semicircle in the anticlockwise direction from \(270^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\) Hence the complete Nyquist Plot is: Check: The given contour encircles two poles in clockwise direction. Hence the mapped nyquist plot should encircle the origin two times in opposite direction of the contour, that is, in anticlockwise direction. Hence, the obtained nyquist plot is correct.

questions.question:
Answer Questions Q7.01.1, Q7.01.2 and Q7.01.3 using the following data. These three questions together carry a total of 5 marks. Consider the open-loop transfer function \[G(s)=\frac{s+1}{s(s-1)}\] The Nyquist contour \(C\) is shown in the figure. The contour has an indentation to the left of the pole at the origin.

What is the encirclement criterion for stability of this system with the type of contour chosen?
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation: The given Nyquist contour is traversed in the clockwise direction. With this choice of contour, a clockwise encirclement of the critical point \((-1,j0)\) is taken as negative. The Nyquist stability criterion is: \(N=P-Z\), where \(N\) is the net clockwise encirclements of \((-1,0)\), \(P\) is the number of right-half-plane poles of the open-loop transfer function and \(Z\) is the number of right-half-plane poles of the closed-loop system. For closed-loop stability, \(Z=0\). Therefore, \[N=2-0=2\] Thus, if the nyquist plot of open-loop transfer function encircles the point \((-1,j0)\) twice in anti clockwise direction, then the system would be stable. Hence, the encirclement criterion for stability of this system with the type of contour chosen is: \[\boxed{N=2}\]

questions.question:
Answer Questions Q7.01.1, Q7.01.2 and Q7.01.3 using the following data. These three questions together carry a total of 5 marks. Consider the open-loop transfer function \[G(s)=\frac{s+1}{s(s-1)}\] The Nyquist contour \(C\) is shown in the figure. The contour has an indentation to the left of the pole at the origin.

Using this criterion determine the range of the gain K of the proportional controller over which the closed loop system in unity feedback will be stable.
questions.explanation: With proportional gain \(K\), the open-loop transfer function is: \[G(s)=\frac{K(s+1)}{s(s-1)}\] The characteristic equation of the closed-loop system is: \[1+G(s)=0\] \[1+\frac{K(s+1)}{s(s-1)}=0\] \[s^2+(K-1)s+K=0\] For stability, all the coefficients should be of same sign. Hence, \[K-1>0,\qquad K>0\] Hence, \(K>1\) \[\boxed{K>1}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A process in a feedback loop with a proportional controller with ultimate gain \(K_u=10\) is oscillating at a frequency of \(P_u=8\,\text{Hz}\). The Ziegler-Nichols setting for the proportional controller is
questions.explanation:
According to the Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop tuning rules, the proportional gain for a P controller is: \[K_p=0.5K_u\] Given, \(K_u=10\), \[K_p=0.5\times10=5\] \[\boxed{(B)\;5}\]
Key points
  • Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop tuning rules: \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Controller} & K_p & T_i & T_d\\ \hline P & 0.5K_u & - & -\\ PI & 0.45K_u & \dfrac{P_u}{1.2} & -\\ PID & 0.6K_u & \dfrac{P_u}{2} & \dfrac{P_u}{8}\\ \hline \end{array}\]
  • The oscillation period (or frequency) is not required for tuning a P controller.
